newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin surgery now an everyday marvel of medicine.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin surgery now an everyday marvel of medicine.

text.p: A surgeon sliced Boris Yeltsin open from neck to belly on Tuesday to expose his heart in the first stage of a lengthy operation requiring great delicacy but which modest medical men dismiss as "glorified plumbing".
Cardiac bypass surgery -- the 65-year-old Russian president needs three or possibly four tissue grafts to improve the blood supply to his heart -- is one of the marvels of modern medicine.

But with hundreds performed daily around the world and a success rate of 95 percent or more, professionals can get blase, leaving it to the layman to retain a sense of wonder that the human heart can be stopped for hours, replumbed like a furred-up washing machine and set pumping again for years of active use.
Since the first heart bypass, by Texan surgeon Michael DeBakey in 1964, the treatment has given new life to millions suffering from one of the Western world's biggest killers.
DeBakey, the now 88-year-old veteran of some 60,000 heart operations, is in Moscow to advise his former pupil, Renat Akchurin, who will operate on Yeltsin.
The 50-year-old Russian, who will perform the surgery at the Cardiology Research Centre, bears a heavy responsibility.
If he fails, Russia could be plunged into a turbulent time of political uncertainty sending jitters around the world.
Akchurin has taken care to counter some of the Kremlin's more flagrant over-optimism, saying that, while relatively straightforward, the operation "is no picnic".
Precise details of the procedure on Yeltsin have not been released but doctors say techniques are similar the world over.
The operation is likely to last five hours or more.

The first incision will cut through the skin and fat on the president's chest to bare the breast bone. The bone will then be swiftly sliced vertically in two with an electric saw and the chest wall clamped open to leave the heart exposed.
Separately, a second surgeon should slice open the Kremlin leader's leg to strip out some 30 cm (a foot) or more of vein.

This will be cut into lengths and grafted in to divert blood around blockages in his heart arteries caused by ischaemia -- a build-up of sediment that down-to-earth doctors compare to the "furring up" of washing machines by calcium deposits in water.
Doctors say Yeltsin also needs some repair work on his mitral heart valve, which can be done during the operation.

A bit of temporary plumbing is then needed so that the heart can be shut down for surgery. Effectively, the lead surgeon short-circuits the heart by means of two plastic tubes that carry blood instead through a heart-lung machine.

As the heart is stopped and kept chilled with cold fluids, this device adds oxygen to the blood and pumps it round the body, allowing the surgeons time to chop into the clogged arteries around it and stitch in the bypasses. Nearby chest arteries can also be dragooned into service as detours.
It sounds simple. About as simple as sewing lengths of macaroni with a sharpened knitting needle. Surgeons need a steady hand, precision instruments and years of training to do it.

Once it is done, doctors can jump-start the presidential heart with an electric shock and the surgeon can check his sutures are holding and the blood is clotting properly. He can then bind the breastbone back together and stitch up the skin.
In one sense, the operation is over. But doctors say the biggest risks in Yeltsin's case may lie immediately afterwards.
The president, whom Akchurin said was being a difficult patient last summer, has been treated for anaemia, thyroid trouble and other problems in weeks of preparation for surgery.
Two German cardiologists from Hannover, specialists in intensive care for heart patients with post-operative complications, are also in Moscow to advise Akchurin's team.

Bypass patients, reinvigorated by their first easy rush of blood in years, can be sitting up within 24 hours. Yeltsin will stay under close observation after the surgery. But his doctors say he could be back at work in a couple of months.
